metadata.title: A SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW OF EVALUATING THE ACCURACY OF NVIVO, R, AND LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS IN THEMATIC ANALYSIS OF INTERVIEW DATA: A COMPARATIVE STUDY

abstract: In response to the growing integration of computational tools in qualitative research, this study presents a systematic comparison of three widely adopted approaches for conducting thematic analysis on qualitative interview data: NVivo (proprietary), R-based text analysis packages (open source), and Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT. Thematic analysis remains a cornerstone of qualitative inquiry, and with increasing reliance on automated methods, it is essential to understand how accurately these tools replicate the depth, nuance, and contextual sensitivity of human-coded analysis. Interview transcripts, selected for their richness in expression and detail, provide a robust dataset for comparative evaluation. Manual thematic coding, grounded in Braun and Clarke's six-phase framework, is employed as the gold standard. Each tool then independently analyzes the same dataset to extract themes and patterns. The resulting outputs are assessed using established metrics such as Precision, Recall, F1 Score, and Thematic Overlap, which quantitatively capture the degree of alignment with the human-coded reference. This evaluation aims not only to identify the comparative strengths and weaknesses of each tool but also to highlight the contexts in which specific tools may be most effective or limited. Moreover, the study delves into the potential of hybrid approaches that combine human judgment with machine-driven analysis to improve both accuracy and efficiency. By systematically mapping the capabilities and limitations of these tools, the research provides valuable, evidence-based guidance for researchers and practitioners navigating the evolving domain of AI-supported qualitative analysis. The findings are intended to support more informed tool selection and promote the thoughtful integration of computational methods into human-centered research workflows.

A SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW OF EVALUATING THE ACCURACY OF NVIVO, R, AND 
LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS IN THEMATIC ANALYSIS OF INTERVIEW DATA: A 
COMPARATIVE STUDY 
 
BC Jayawardana1, AS Withanaarachchi2, S Jayalal3 and R Abeysekara4        
                                                           
Abstract 
 
In response to the growing integration of computational tools in qualitative research, this study presents a 
systematic comparison of three widely adopted approaches for conducting thematic analysis on qualitative 
interview data: NVivo (proprietary), R based text analysis packages (open source), and Large Language Models 
(LLMs) such as ChatGPT. Thematic analysis remains a cornerstone of qualitative inquiry, and with increasing 
reliance on automated methods, it is essential to understand how accurately these tools replicate the depth, nuance, 
and contextual sensitivity of human coded analysis. Interview transcripts, selected for their richness in expression 
and detail, provide a robust dataset for comparative evaluation. Manual thematic coding, grounded in Braun and 
Clarke’s six phase framework, is employed as the gold standard. Each tool then independently analyzes the same 
dataset to extract themes and patterns. The resulting outputs are assessed using established metrics such as 
Precision, Recall, F1 Score, and Thematic Overlap, which quantitatively capture the degree of alignment with the 
human coded reference. This evaluation aims not only to identify the comparative strengths and weaknesses of 
each tool but also to highlight the contexts in which specific tools may be most effective or limited. Moreover, the 
study delves into the potential of hybrid approaches that combine human judgment with machine driven analysis 
to improve both accuracy and efficiency. By systematically mapping the capabilities and limitations of these tools, 
the research provides valuable, evidence based guidance for researchers and practitioners navigating the evolving 
domain of AI supported qualitative analysis. The findings are intended to support more informed tool selection 
and promote the thoughtful integration of computational methods into human centered research workflows. 
 
Keywords: Accuracy Assessment, Hybrid Methods, Large Language Models, Qualitative Research, Thematic

Introduction 
Background of Study 
Thematic analysis (TA) is a foundational method in qualitative research, facilitating the identification, analysis, 
and reporting of patterns within data. Braun and Clarke's (Braun & Clarke, 2006) six-phase framework comprising 
familiarization with data, generating initial codes, searching for themes, reviewing themes, defining and naming 
themes, and producing the report has become a widely adopted approach due to its flexibility and systematic 
nature. Traditionally, TA is conducted manually, requiring significant time and interpretative effort from 
researchers. 
 
The advent of computational tools has introduced new avenues for conducting TA. Software like NVivo offers 
functionalities for organizing and analysing qualitative data, enabling researchers to code and retrieve data 
efficiently (Jackson & Bazeley, 2019). Similarly, R an open-source statistical computing environment, provides 
packages such as 'tm' and 'topicmodels' that support text mining and topic modelling, facilitating automated 
thematic extraction (Feinerer et al., 2008). More recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) like OpenAI's GPT 
series have demonstrated capabilities in understanding and generating human like text, presenting opportunities 
for automating aspects of qualitative analysis. 
 
Despite these advancements, questions remain regarding the accuracy and reliability of these tools in replicating 
the depth and nuance of human led TA. Comparative studies assessing the performance of NVivo, R based tools, 
and LLMs against manual coding are limited, necessitating systematic evaluations to inform methodological 
choices in qualitative research. 
 
Problem Statement 
The integration of computational tools into thematic analysis presents both opportunities and challenges. While 
tools like NVivo, R based packages, and LLMs can enhance efficiency and scalability, their ability to accurately 
replicate human-led thematic analysis remains uncertain. There is a need for systematic evaluation of these tools 
to determine their accuracy, reliability and suitability for qualitative research. 
 
Literature Review 
NVivo is a proprietary qualitative data analysis software designed to assist researchers in managing and analysing 
unstructured data. It offers features such as coding, querying, and visualization tools that support the thematic 
analysis process (Jackson & Bazeley, 2019). Studies have highlighted NVivo's utility in enhancing the efficiency 
of data organization and retrieval. However, the software's effectiveness is contingent upon the researcher's input, 
and it does not inherently perform thematic analysis without human guidance (Zamawe, 2015). 
 
Although NVivo supports both manual and automated coding functions, this review did not specifically 
distinguish between studies based on the type of coding employed. Existing methodological literature indicates 
that automated coding is useful for quickly identifying broad patterns or categories, whereas manual coding offers 
greater depth and sensitivity to contextual nuances (Paulus, 2023). Prior studies have emphasized that while 
automated methods may enhance efficiency during the initial stages of analysis, they often require additional 
manual intervention to produce well-developed and coherent thematic results (Mortelmans, 2025). The suitability 
of each method ultimately depends on the analytical objectives and the level of interpretive depth required. Future 
reviews may consider directly comparing studies that rely on manual versus automated coding in NVivo to better 
understand the implications for analytical quality and research outcomes. 
 
R provides a suite of packages for text analysis, including 'tm' for text mining and 'topicmodels' for topic modelling 
using algorithms like Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Feinerer et al., 2008). These tools enable automated 
identification of themes within large text corpora. While R based methods offer scalability and reproducibility, 
they may lack the contextual sensitivity inherent in human analysis, potentially overlooking nuanced themes 
(Grimmer & Stewart, 2013). 
 
LLMs, such as GPT-3 and GPT-4, have shown promise in automating aspects of qualitative analysis.(Dai et al., 
2023) introduced an "LLM-in-the-loop" framework, demonstrating that LLMs can assist in generating initial 
codes and themes, reducing the time and labour associated with manual coding. GPT-4 was able to generate 
thematic outputs that closely aligned with those produced by legal professionals in empirical research contexts 
(Drápal et al., 2023). However, concerns about LLMs include potential biases, lack of transparency in decision-
making processes, and the need for human oversight to ensure validity (De Paoli, 2024). 
 
The growing capabilities of LLMs in conducting thematic analysis have shown significant potential for enhancing 
efficiency and scalability beyond what is achievable through traditional manual methods. A recent comparative

study involving nine generative AI models including ChatGPT o1-Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini Advanced 
demonstrated high levels of accuracy, with several models achieving complete thematic alignment with expert-
coded benchmarks (Jaccard Index = 1.00) (Bennis & Mouwafaq, 2025). The authors also introduced the “Fractal 
Circle of Vulnerabilities” framework, which exemplifies how LLMs can support the development of nuanced 
conceptual models in qualitative inquiry. However, the study was domain-specific, focusing on the psychosocial 
effects of cutaneous leishmaniasis and employing a grounded theory approach. It did not include direct 
comparisons between LLM-generated outputs and those produced by traditional tools such as NVivo or R across 
broader qualitative datasets. This limitation points to a critical gap in the literature, emphasizing the need for 
systematic evaluations that assess LLMs alongside established CAQDAS and statistical text analysis tools, a gap 
that the present review seeks to address. 
 
Aim and Scope 
This systematic literature review aims to critically evaluate and compare the accuracy and effectiveness of three 
widely used tools NVivo, R based text analysis packages, and LLMs such as ChatGPT in performing thematic 
analysis on qualitative interview data. By systematically examining existing research and synthesizing evidence 
on these computational approaches, this review seeks to illuminate how well these tools replicate or complement 
human-led thematic coding, particularly in identifying patterns, themes, and contextual meanings from rich 
interview transcripts. 
The study’s scope includes assessing methodological approaches, analytic outputs, and evaluation metrics 
reported in the literature to provide nuanced insights for qualitative researchers selecting suitable analytical tools. 
Additionally, this review explores the potential for hybrid methods that integrate human expertise with AI 
capabilities to enhance accuracy and efficiency in qualitative data analysis. 
 
Research Objectives 
RO1: To systematically identify and categorize the capabilities and limitations of NVivo, R based tools, and LLMs 
in performing thematic analysis on qualitative interview data. 
 
This objective focuses on understanding the specific functionalities and analytical scopes each tool offers and how 
they align with qualitative research needs. 
RO2: To compare the accuracy and validity of thematic outputs produced by NVivo, R based packages, and LLMs 
against manual human coded thematic analysis. 
 
This involves synthesizing evaluation metrics such as Precision, Recall, F1 Score, and thematic overlap reported 
in empirical studies. 
 
RO3: To explore emerging trends, challenges, and opportunities in combining human expertise with AI assisted 
thematic analysis methods. This includes identifying hybrid approaches that leverage strengths of both human 
coders and computational tools to improve qualitative analysis outcomes. 
 
Research Questions 
RQ1: What are the reported strengths and limitations of NVivo, R-based text analysis tools, and Large Language 
Models in conducting thematic analysis of interview data? 
 
RQ2: How do the thematic analysis results generated by these tools compare in accuracy and thematic overlap to 
manual human coding? 
 
RQ3: What are the current trends and prospects in integrating human qualitative expertise with AI powered tools 
for thematic analysis? 
 
By systematically consolidating and critically evaluating evidence across these dimensions, this review aims to 
guide researchers in selecting and applying appropriate tools for qualitative thematic analysis while highlighting 
directions for advancing computational qualitative methods. 
 
Methodology 
This systematic literature review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines (Page et al., 
2021) to ensure transparency, reproducibility, and methodological rigor throughout the study. The primary 
objective was to explore and evaluate the accuracy and comparative effectiveness of qualitative analysis tools 
NVivo, R, and Large Language Models in conducting thematic analysis of interview-based qualitative data.

Search Strategy and Data Sources 
To ensure comprehensive coverage of the literature across both computational and social science domains, a multi-
database search strategy was adopted. Five electronic databases were selected based on their disciplinary 
relevance, indexing coverage, and support for advanced filtering and search functionalities. These included: 
Google Scholar, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, ACM Digital Library. 
 
Search Terms and Filtering 
A Boolean search strategy was developed and refined for each database, combining synonyms and related terms 
to capture relevant publications. Queries were customized to comply with the syntax and filtering capabilities of 
each platform. The core search string included combinations of the following terms: 
 
("NVivo" OR "R programming" OR "R software" OR "Large Language Model*" OR "LLM" OR "ChatGPT" OR 
"GPT" OR "BERT" OR "Transformer model*") AND ("thematic analysis" OR "qualitative analysis" OR 
"qualitative coding" OR "content analysis") AND ("interview data" OR "qualitative data" OR "text data" OR 
"open-ended responses") 
This query was slightly customized per database to match each platform’s syntax and filtering capabilities as 
indicated in the Prisma flow diagram in Fig. 1. 
Where applicable, results were filtered to include: 
• 
Publication year: January 2020 to April 2025 
• 
Language: English only 
• 
Publication type: Peer-reviewed journal articles and conference proceedings 
 
Screening and Selection Process 
The screening process followed the PRISMA protocol, as illustrated in the PRISMA flow diagram. A total of 9,178 
records were initially retrieved from all databases. In the identification phase, the following records were 
excluded: 
• 
Duplicate entries: 1,203 
• 
Publications before 2020: 1,623 
• 
Non-English publications: 97 
• 
Google Scholar results beyond the 20th page: 2,865 
• 
Documents not classified as journal articles or conference papers: 2,387 
After initial filtering, 1,003 records remained for title and abstract screening. Of these, 695 records were excluded 
due to lack of relevance to the research questions or focus area. From the remaining 308 studies, full texts were 
sought. 59 articles were excluded due to inaccessible full text. A total of 249 full text articles were assessed for 
eligibility. Among these, 219 were excluded for the following reasons: 
• 
Conceptual or theoretical papers without empirical evaluation 
• 
Studies that did not involve NVivo, R, or LLMs in thematic analysis 
• 
Lack of methodological detail, such as datasets or evaluation metrics 
Ultimately, 32 primary studies were included in the final synthesis.

The extracted data were analysed thematically and quantitatively to identify methodological patterns, comparative 
insights, and emerging trends in the use of AI and statistical software for qualitative data analysis. 
 
Results and discussion 
Overview of Study Selection and Publication Trends 
The distribution of selected studies over the five-year period (Fig. 2.) reveals a clear upward trajectory in scholarly 
attention toward computational tools for thematic analysis. Initial interest appeared modest, with relatively few 
studies published in the early years, reflecting the nascent stage of integrating NVivo, R based tools, and LLMs 
into qualitative research workflows. However, a notable surge in publications is observed in more recent years, 
particularly from 2023 onwards. This increase aligns with broader advancements in natural language processing 
and the widespread adoption of AI driven methodologies across the social sciences. The pronounced rise in 2024 
suggests growing confidence in the applicability of these tools, alongside an expanding body of empirical 
evaluations. Furthermore, the emergence of studies in early 2025 indicates sustained scholarly engagement and 
evolving methodological curiosity. Collectively, the publication trend underscores a shifting paradigm in 
qualitative research, where traditional manual analysis is increasingly complemented or augmented by 
computational approaches, reflecting both technological maturation and methodological innovation. 
 
Figure 02: Distribution of Studies by Years 
 
The reviewed literature spans a diverse range of publication types (Fig. 3.) and geographic origins (Fig. 4.), 
reflecting the global interest in advancing computational approaches to qualitative research. A notable proportion 
of studies were presented in conference proceedings, underscoring the dynamic and evolving nature of this 
interdisciplinary field. These contributions originate from various countries, including technologically advanced 
regions such as the United States, Singapore, and Ireland, as well as emerging research hubs like India, China, 
and Ethiopia. This geographical distribution suggests a broadening engagement with automated, and AI assisted 
thematic analysis methods across different research environments and academic traditions. Additionally, the 
inclusion of both conference papers and peer-reviewed journal articles highlights the interplay between emerging 
innovations and established scholarly discourse. Such diversity not only enhances the richness of the evidence 
base but also supports a more comprehensive understanding of how tools like NVivo, R based packages and LLMs 
are evaluated and applied within different methodological and cultural contexts in qualitative research. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Dataset Characteristics and Interview Modalities 
 
 
 
Most datasets utilized semi structured interviews, though some also incorporated open-ended survey responses, 
focus group data, or organizational documents. Studies in healthcare often used rich narrative data for example,

one conducted in Lesotho involved 41 participants (Nkabane-Nkholongo et al., 2023; Rajput et al., 2024), while 
another U.S.-based wellness study included over 52,000 words of transcript data (Jalali & Akhavan, 2024; Li et 
al., 2024; Mwangi, 2023). In contrast, research in business and technology tended to focus on document analysis 
or review mining (e.g., 200 abstracts or 193 coded product reviews). English was the dominant language of 
analysis, though a few studies used datasets in Chinese or Sesotho. Dataset sizes ranged widely from single in-
depth interviews (Bhardwaj & Agrawal, 2021; Chen, 2020, 2020; H. Zhao et al., 2023) to thousands of responses 
(Ahamat et al., 2023), and formats included DOCX, PDF, and JSON files (Alam et al., 2024). 
Thematic analysis across the reviewed literature indicates that semi structured interviews were the most prevalent 
data collection method, utilized in approximately 62% of the studies included (Fig. 5.). This approach offers a 
balance between guided inquiry and exploratory flexibility, making it particularly well suited for examining user 
experiences, healthcare interactions, and educational practices (Genus et al., 2021; Kurt & Kurt, 2024; 
Simaremare et al., 2024). Unstructured interviews were employed in seven studies, typically within exploratory 
or ethnographic frameworks (Liu & Li, 2022) while structured interviews were the least common, appearing in 
only four cases due to their rigid format (Li et al., 2024). 
 
Figure 05. Frequency of Interview Types Used in Studies 
 
Interview data were drawn primarily from four domains as social sciences, business, healthcare and education 
(Fig. 6.). Education emerged as the dominant domain, covering themes such as digital communication, 
organizational behavior, and public engagement (Xu & Jumaat, 2024). Healthcare related studies focused on areas 
like mental health, reproductive services and patient experiences (Hussein et al., 2023). The social science and 
business domains explored teacher training, e learning innovations, and the integration of gamification in 
pedagogy (Freitas et al., 2024).

Manual Coding as the Gold Standard 
Manual thematic coding was generally considered the gold standard against which tool generated outputs were 
compared (Q. Wang et al., 2025). While nearly all studies used human coders to develop benchmark themes, only 
a minority reported inter coder reliability metrics such as Cohen’s Kappa or Krippendorff’s Alpha. Most studies 
relied on coding consensus through discussion among small research teams. Widely adopted frameworks included 
Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis model and grounded theory-based approaches (Kurt & Kurt, 2024; 
Simaremare et al., 2024). Challenges identified in manual coding processes included subjectivity, labour intensity, 
and time consumption (Doszhan et al., 2022). 
Beyond inter-coder differences, several studies implicitly raise concerns about intra-coder inconsistency the 
tendency for the same individual to apply codes differently over time or in varying contexts. Such inconsistencies 
may arise due to factors like cognitive fatigue, evolving familiarity with the dataset, or shifts in interpretive stance 
throughout the analytic process (Doszhan et al., 2022; Fitkov-Norris & Kocheva, 2023). Although few studies 
formally assessed this dimension, intra-coder variability represents a potential limitation in the use of manual 
coding as a benchmark for evaluating computational tools, especially in cases where methodological transparency 
and coder reflexivity are insufficiently reported (De Paoli, 2024; Nkabane-Nkholongo et al., 2023). 
Manual coding was applied as a gold standard in 74.19% of the studies reviewed (Fig. 7), reaffirming the 
foundational role of human interpretation in qualitative analysis (Jangjarat et al., 2023). Several studies 
underscored the necessity of human coding, particularly when evaluating or validating outputs from automated 
tools (X. Wang et al., 2024). This practice ensured that subtle nuances and contextual meanings were preserved 
throughout the analytic process. 
Among the studies employing human coders, 14 reported the use of multiple coders to enhance the reliability of 
the thematic extraction process. However, only a subset reported inter-coder agreement using statistical measures. 
For instance, a Cohen’s kappa score of 0.72 was documented, reflecting moderate to strong agreement (Jangjarat 
et al., 2023; Kurt & Kurt, 2024; Nkabane-Nkholongo et al., 2023). Common analytical frameworks referenced 
across these studies included Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis model (De Paoli, 2024) indicating 
methodological consistency. 
The data reveals a strong inclination toward using human coded benchmarks to assess the performance of 
computational tools in thematic analysis. Of the 32 studies reviewed, 23 incorporated manually coded themes as 
a gold standard, while the remaining seven did not report the use of any human coded reference. This highlights 
the continued reliance on traditional human-led thematic analysis as a validation baseline in evaluating the 
accuracy of automated tools (Nkabane-Nkholongo et al., 2023). 
 
 
Figure 07: Frequency of Human-Coded Benchmarks Across Studies 
Further analysis of reporting practices shows inconsistency in documenting coder involvement and agreement. 
Specifically, nine studies mentioned the number of human coders involved but did not provide inter coder 
reliability statistics (Fig. 8.). Five studies reported both the number of coders and agreement metrics, such as

Tools and Techniques for Thematic Analysis 
NVivo was the most frequently applied software, valued for its visual and hierarchical coding capabilities. Several 
studies used it as a standalone tool, while others combined it with R or manual annotation. R was employed mainly 
in studies using text mining, topic modelling (e.g., LDA, NMF), or sentiment analysis through packages such as 
tm, tidytext, and quanteda (Ahamat et al., 2023; Arya & Kulkarni, 2024; Li et al., 2024; Srivastava et al., 2021). 
LLMs, including ChatGPT and Sentence-BERT, were introduced in seven studies, commonly used for clustering, 
co coding, or preliminary theme exploration (Gronneberg & Nygard, 2022). Approximately one-third of the 
reviewed studies adopted hybrid strategies, integrating NVivo with R or combining R-based methods with LLM 
generated outputs (Rajput et al., 2024). 
 
NVivo emerged as the most widely adopted tool, featured in 19 studies (Fig. 9.). Its utility in supporting visual 
analysis, theme mapping, and qualitative node management was frequently cited (Chen, 2020; Mallion et al., 
2021). LLMs including ChatGPT, GPT-3, and BERT were employed in 8 studies, primarily for their capabilities 
in context-aware theme extraction and scalable content summarization (Alam et al., 2024; Allen & Thompson, 
2024). In contrast, R-based packages such as tm, quanteda, and tidytext were applied in 5 studies, favored for their 
customizability and compatibility with academic workflows (Li et al., 2024). 
 
 
Figure 09: Frequency of Tools Used in Studies 
Among LLMs, ChatGPT was the most utilized (Fig. 10.), primarily in tasks involving initial code generation and 
textual summarization (Allen & Thompson, 2024). Other models, such as BERT and GPT-3, were deployed for 
analyzing feedback and user sentiment, particularly within social media datasets (Allen & Thompson, 2024). A 
notable inclusion was LLaMA, used in one study, indicating emerging interest in open-source LLM alternatives 
(De Paoli, 2024).

Several studies employed hybrid analytical pipelines to combine the strengths of both human and computational 
methods (Fig. 11.). Six studies integrated NVivo with manual coding, while three adopted LLM and R-based 
combinations to enhance coding scalability and depth (De Paoli, 2024; Q. Wang et al., 2025). Additionally, five 
studies utilized human-in-the-loop strategies, where LLM generated codes were reviewed and refined by 
researchers, reflecting a growing trend toward collaborative and interpretable AI assisted thematic analysis. 
 
 
Figure 11: Percentages of Using multiple Tools in Studies 
 
Evaluation Methods for Accuracy 
The evaluation of tool performance varied significantly across studies. Traditional quantitative metrics such as 
precision, recall, and F1 score were rarely reported. Instead, most studies used qualitative benchmarks, such as 
thematic overlap with human-coded results, novelty of insights, or clarity of categories (Allen & Thompson, 
2024). A few studies applied numerical measures of thematic match; for instance, T-Lab achieved an 86% match 
rate, while IRaMuTeQ reported 58% when compared to human coding (Fitkov-Norris & Kocheva, 2023). NVivo 
was often used more as a visual aid or organizational platform than as a tool for generating themes to be evaluated 
against ground truth. 
 
Comparative Accuracy Across Tools 
Comparative analyses yielded varied outcomes. LLMs such as ChatGPT often generated novel or additional 
themes not detected by human coders, suggesting potential advantages in exploratory contexts (Freitas et al., 2024; 
Q. Wang et al., 2025). However, concerns about transparency and reproducibility of AI outputs were commonly 
noted. R text analysis packages, especially when coupled with Sentence-BERT or NMF algorithms, achieved high 
performance scores (up to 87.4% F1 score) but required extensive preprocessing and manual oversight (Alam et

Limitations 
This systematic review identifies several critical challenges associated with applying NVivo, R based solutions, 
and LLMs for thematic analysis of interview based qualitative data. 
• 
Inconsistent methodologies - The reviewed studies exhibit significant variation in dataset design, coding 
approaches, and evaluation criteria, making it difficult to draw direct comparisons or synthesize findings 
effectively. 
• 
Language and dataset constraints - A heavy focus on English language data restricts the utility of these 
tools in multilingual settings or with non-English transcripts. 
• 
Lack of transparency in LLMs - Tools such as ChatGPT and GPT-4 operate as opaque systems, offering 
limited visibility into how themes are derived raising concerns around interpretability, trust, and 
auditability. 
• 
Underuse of quantitative accuracy measures - Few studies employed robust evaluation metrics (e.g. 
Precision, Recall, F1 Score); instead, many relied on narrative or subjective assessments, which 
undermines the replicability of findings. 
• 
Steep learning curve and usability challenges - NVivo and R require considerable technical expertise, 
while prompt variability in LLMs may result in inconsistent outputs and reduced ease of use. 
• 
Narrow data scope - Some research drew on small or narrowly defined datasets, reducing the external 
validity and limiting the broader application of their conclusions.

Recommendations 
To strengthen the quality, comparability and real-world relevance of computational thematic analysis, the 
following recommendations are proposed. 
• 
Establish multilingual, open-access benchmark datasets - Develop standardized, well annotated interview 
datasets in multiple languages to improve accessibility and support reproducible research across 
linguistic boundaries. 
• 
Implement consistent evaluation standards - Enhancing the reliability and comparability of thematic 
analyses requires future studies to utilize standardized metrics like F1 Score, Thematic Overlap, and 
inter-coder agreement (e.g., Cohen’s Kappa).  
• 
Equally important is the assessment of intra-coder consistency, as temporal variations in individual 
coding can affect the validity of human benchmarks used to evaluate automated methods.Leverage 
hybrid analysis models - Combine AI based approaches (e.g., LLM-assisted coding) with human 
validation to capitalize on computational efficiency while preserving thematic depth and contextual 
accuracy. 
• 
Enhance reporting transparency - Encourage comprehensive reporting of methodological details 
including dataset characteristics, coding workflows, tool configurations, and LLM prompts to foster 
replicability and knowledge sharing. 
• 
Support integration and interoperability - Design interoperable tool ecosystems such as plugins or APIs 
that enable seamless transitions and data flow between NVivo, R platforms, and LLM interfaces, 
improving user experience and analytical productivity. 
 
Conclusion  
This review affirms that while NVivo, R based packages, and LLMs each offer distinct advantages, no tool is 
universally superior for all thematic analysis contexts. LLMs were particularly effective in handling emotionally 
rich or abstract interview data, showing higher thematic recall and acceptable precision. R based packages proved 
well suited for structured text analysis and statistical modelling, while NVivo stood out for its intuitive 
visualizations and code organization features. 
 
Nevertheless, human coded thematic frameworks continue to serve as the strongest benchmark, emphasizing the 
enduring value of human interpretation in qualitative research. The study underscores the necessity for context 
aware tool selection, guided by factors such as dataset size, research aims, and linguistic requirements. These 
insights are vital as qualitative research becomes increasingly intertwined with AI driven methodologies. This 
review has successfully addressed these considerations and fulfilled all the stated research objectives. 
 
Future Directions  
Moving forward, research in computational thematic analysis should prioritize the development of standardized 
evaluation frameworks and benchmark datasets. These efforts should be coupled with the creation of cross 
linguistic corpora and API enabled tool integrations, particularly between LLMs and traditional platforms like 
NVivo or R. Such integration could enable real-time co-coding and streamline the human AI collaboration process. 
 
Additionally, the field would benefit from focused studies on LLM interpretability and explainability, helping to 
demystify how themes are generated. Further exploration into disciplinary variation for example, how LLM 
performance differs between healthcare, education, and business domains could inform more precise tool 
deployment. Investment in AI literacy and training for qualitative researchers is also critical to ensure ethical, 
responsible, and technically sound use of computational tools.

key_findings.claim: Hybrid approaches combining human expertise with computational tools yielded the most accurate and interpretable results in thematic analysis, outperforming any single tool used alone.
key_findings.context: Synthesized across 32 primary studies; approximately one-third adopted hybrid strategies integrating NVivo with R or combining R-based methods with LLM outputs.

key_findings.claim: R-based text analysis packages (e.g., Sentence-BERT, NMF) achieved the highest reported quantitative accuracy scores among computational tools, reaching up to 87.4% F1 score.
key_findings.quantitative_result: F1 score up to 87.4% (Alam et al., 2024; F. Zhao et al., 2024)
key_findings.context: Achieved in specific studies using structured text; required extensive preprocessing and manual oversight.

key_findings.claim: LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT, GPT-4) regularly produced themes beyond those identified by human coders, suggesting advantages in exploratory thematic analysis contexts.
key_findings.context: Reported across 8 studies using LLMs; numerical performance inconsistently reported; LLMs featured in studies by Freitas et al. (2024) and Wang et al. (2025).

key_findings.claim: Nine generative AI models (including ChatGPT o1-Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini Advanced) achieved complete thematic alignment with expert-coded benchmarks in one domain-specific study.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Jaccard Index = 1.00 for several models (Bennis & Mouwafaq, 2025)
key_findings.context: Domain-specific study on psychosocial effects of cutaneous leishmaniasis using grounded theory; did not include NVivo or R comparisons.

key_findings.claim: NVivo was the most widely adopted tool across reviewed studies but lacked scalability and automatic topic detection, functioning primarily as a visual and organizational aid rather than an autonomous theme generator.
key_findings.context: NVivo quantitative accuracy metrics generally absent; T-Lab (a related tool) achieved 86% match rate and IRaMuTeQ reported 58% vs human coding (Fitkov-Norris & Kocheva, 2023).

key_findings.claim: Manual human thematic coding was used as the gold standard benchmark in 74.19% of the 32 reviewed studies, but inter-coder reliability was inconsistently reported.
key_findings.quantitative_result: 74.19% of studies used human-coded benchmarks; Cohen's kappa of 0.72 reported in a subset; only 5 of 32 studies reported both coder count and agreement metrics; 15 studies reported neither.
key_findings.context: Human expert inter-coder agreement typically falls between 70-85% across studies.

key_findings.claim: Publication output on computational thematic analysis tools surged markedly from 2023 onwards, with sustained growth into 2025, reflecting rapid adoption of AI-driven qualitative methods.
key_findings.context: Publication trend derived from distribution of 32 studies across 2020-2025.

key_findings.claim: Semi-structured interviews were the dominant data collection modality in the reviewed literature, used in approximately 62% of included studies.
key_findings.context: Across 32 primary studies spanning social sciences, business, healthcare, and education domains.

key_findings.claim: Traditional quantitative evaluation metrics (precision, recall, F1 score) were rarely reported in reviewed studies; most relied on qualitative benchmarks such as thematic overlap or narrative assessment.
key_findings.context: This underuse of standardized metrics undermines replicability and comparability across tool evaluation studies.

key_findings.claim: No single computational tool is universally superior for all thematic analysis contexts; optimal tool selection depends on dataset size, research aims, and linguistic requirements.
key_findings.context: Synthesized conclusion across 32 studies; LLMs excel with abstract/emotional data, R packages suit structured statistical analysis, NVivo is best for visualization and code organization.

llm_extraction.methods_summary: PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic literature review. Five electronic databases searched (Google Scholar, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, ACM Digital Library) using Boolean search strings combining NVivo/R/LLM terms with thematic analysis terms. Publication years restricted to January 2020–April 2025; English only; peer-reviewed journal articles and conference proceedings only. Of 9,178 initially retrieved records, 32 primary empirical studies were included after staged screening (removal of duplicates, pre-2020 publications, non-English papers, inaccessible full texts, and studies lacking empirical evaluation of NVivo/R/LLMs in thematic analysis). Data extraction covered: analytical tools used, interview data type and source, accuracy metrics, methodological frameworks, nature of comparison, and key findings. Extracted data analyzed thematically and quantitatively.
llm_extraction.limitations: 1) Inconsistent methodologies across reviewed studies make direct comparisons difficult. 2) Heavy focus on English-language datasets limits generalizability to multilingual or non-English contexts. 3) LLM outputs lack transparency in how themes are derived, raising concerns about interpretability and auditability. 4) Underuse of standardized quantitative evaluation metrics (precision, recall, F1); most studies used subjective or narrative assessments. 5) Steep learning curves for NVivo and R; prompt variability in LLMs yields inconsistent outputs. 6) Some studies used small or narrowly defined datasets, limiting external validity. 7) The review itself did not distinguish between manual and automated NVivo coding modes, which may conflate different analytical qualities. 8) Intra-coder inconsistency in human gold standard coding was rarely formally assessed, potentially undermining benchmark validity.

relationships.description: This review extends Bennis & Mouwafaq (2025) by situating their finding of high LLM thematic accuracy (Jaccard=1.00) within a broader comparative context that includes NVivo and R-based tools, which that study did not address.

Supports Dai et al. (2023)'s 'LLM-in-the-loop' framework finding that LLMs can reduce time and labour of manual coding, as this review's synthesis confirms LLMs offer efficiency advantages in exploratory thematic contexts.
Corroborates De Paoli (2024)'s concerns about transparency and reproducibility limitations of LLMs in inductive thematic analysis.
Builds on Fitkov-Norris & Kocheva (2023)'s reported accuracy figures (T-Lab 86%, IRaMuTeQ 58%) by contextualizing them within a 32-study comparative synthesis across NVivo, R, and LLMs.

methodology_details.approach: PRISMA 2020 systematic literature review synthesizing empirical studies comparing NVivo, R-based text analysis packages, and LLMs for thematic analysis of qualitative interview data against human-coded benchmarks.
datasets: 32 primary empirical studies (2020-2025) sourced from Google Scholar, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, ACM Digital Library

Underlying study datasets included semi-structured interview transcripts, open-ended survey responses, focus group data, and organizational documents across healthcare, education, social science, and business domains
methodology_details.reproducibility_notes: PRISMA 2020 guidelines followed for transparency and reproducibility of the review process itself. However, reproducibility of underlying primary studies is noted as poor due to inconsistent reporting of methodological details, tool configurations, and LLM prompts across the literature.

domain_specific_fields.benchmark: Manual human thematic coding using Braun & Clarke's six-phase framework as gold standard; inter-coder agreement (Cohen's kappa ~0.72) used in subset of studies
domain_specific_fields.metrics: F1 Score (up to 87.4% for R-based methods), Thematic Overlap, Precision, Recall, Cohen's Kappa, Krippendorff's Alpha, Jaccard Index (1.00 achieved by multiple LLMs in Bennis & Mouwafaq 2025), match rate (T-Lab 86%, IRaMuTeQ 58%)
domain_specific_fields.model_architecture: NVivo (proprietary CAQDAS); R packages: tm, topicmodels (LDA), tidytext, quanteda, Sentence-BERT, NMF; LLMs: ChatGPT (GPT-3, GPT-4, o1-Pro), Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini Advanced, BERT, LLaMA
domain_specific_fields.dataset: Synthesis of 32 empirical studies; underlying datasets include semi-structured interviews (62% of studies), unstructured interviews (~22%), structured interviews (~13%); domains: education, healthcare, social science, business; dataset sizes ranged from single in-depth interviews to >52,000 words of transcript or thousands of survey responses
